nameStory: The White Wagtail gets its name from its distinctive habit of constantly wagging its long tail up and down while walking and feeding. The 'white' part refers to the prominent white markings on its face, belly, and outer tail feathers that flash conspicuously as it moves.
description: The White Wagtail is a sleek, robin-sized songbird with a striking black and white pattern and an extra-long tail that's always in motion. It has a black back, white belly, and bold black and white head pattern that gives it a crisp, clean appearance. This elegant bird walks rather than hops, constantly pumping its tail as it searches for insects on the ground.

idTips.label: Tail wagging behavior
idTips.description: The most obvious feature - watch for the constant up-and-down pumping motion of the long, slender tail, happening almost nonstop as the bird moves

idTips.label: Walking gait
idTips.description: Walks gracefully across open ground rather than hopping like most songbirds, with a smooth, purposeful stride

idTips.label: Black and white pattern
idTips.description: Clean, contrasting colors with black back, white belly, and distinctive black and white head markings that look almost geometric

idTips.label: Ground foraging
idTips.description: Feeds by walking on bare ground, pavement, or short grass, making quick darts to snatch up small insects

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found in open areas near water or human activity - parking lots, beaches, fields, and waterfront areas where it can easily spot prey

habitat: In New England, White Wagtails are extremely rare visitors, typically found along coastal areas, open fields near water, or around human developments like parking lots and airports. They prefer areas with bare ground or very short vegetation where they can easily spot and chase insects, often near ponds, streams, or tidal areas.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring vagrant, most likely to appear during migration periods in April or May near coastal areas or open fields.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in summer as they don't breed in New England, though a vagrant could theoretically appear.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely than spring for vagrant appearances, typically September through October during fall migration.
seasonality.winter: Very unlikely to be seen in winter, as most migrate to warmer climates, though climate change could bring surprises.

funFact: With only 4 recorded sightings in all of New England, seeing a White Wagtail here would be like winning the birding lottery - they're so rare that each appearance becomes legendary among local birdwatchers and gets reported in rare bird alerts across the region!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Pied Wagtail (a subspecies) or even a misidentified mockingbird, but no other New England bird constantly wags its tail while walking on the ground. The tail-wagging behavior combined with the ground-walking gait makes it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
contextualKnowledge: The White Wagtail is actually a complex of subspecies, with the Pied Wagtail being the form found in Britain and Ireland. Any White Wagtail reaching New England would likely be from European or Alaskan populations, making it an extraordinary transatlantic vagrant.
compareHints: White Wagtails are the only members of their genus recorded in New England, but they're related to pipits in the same family. Unlike pipits, which tend to be more streaky brown and prefer to stay hidden in grass, White Wagtails are boldly patterned in black and white and prefer open, bare areas where they can be easily seen.
